claim: Truncating mutations in the giant sarcomeric protein Titin result in dilated cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy.
source: Truncating mutations in the giant sarcomeric protein Titin result in dilated cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The most severely affected dilated cardiomyopathy patients harbor Titin truncations in the C-terminal two-thirds of the protein.
source: The most severely affected dilated cardiomyopathy patients harbor Titin truncations in the C-terminal two-thirds of the protein, suggesting that mutation position might influence disease mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Herman et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2015) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: Six zebrafish lines with Titin truncations in the N-terminal and C-terminal regions were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, we generated six zebrafish lines with Titin truncations in the N-terminal and C-terminal regions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental generation of these lines in the Methods section.

claim: All six targeted exons were constitutive in both cardiac and skeletal muscle.
source: Although all exons were constitutive, C-terminal mutations caused severe myopathy whereas N-terminal mutations demonstrated mild phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data showing PSI values >0.99 for all mutated exons (Table 1, Figure 2C).

claim: C-terminal mutations caused severe myopathy whereas N-terminal mutations demonstrated mild phenotypes.
source: Although all exons were constitutive, C-terminal mutations caused severe myopathy whereas N-terminal mutations demonstrated mild phenotypes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunostaining (Figure 2B) and motility assays (Video 2).

claim: Neither N-terminal nor C-terminal mutation types acted as a dominant negative.
source: Surprisingly, neither mutation type acted as a dominant negative.
evidence: This is supported by morpholino knockdown experiments showing that introducing an upstream frameshift did not rescue skeletal muscle architecture in C-terminal mutants (Figure 3B).

claim: A conserved internal promoter exists at the precise position where divergence in disease severity occurs.
source: Instead, we found a conserved internal promoter at the precise position where divergence in disease severity occurs, with the resulting protein product partially rescuing N-terminal truncations.
evidence: This is supported by 5'-RACE experiments, RNA-Seq data showing read accumulation, and chromatin accessibility data (Figure 4).

claim: The protein product from the internal promoter partially rescues N-terminal truncations.
source: Instead, we found a conserved internal promoter at the precise position where divergence in disease severity occurs, with the resulting protein product partially rescuing N-terminal truncations.
evidence: This is supported by protein gel electrophoresis showing the Cronos isoform in wild-type and N-terminal mutants but not C-terminal mutants (Figure 5A), and morpholino knockdown of the internal promoter disrupting skeletal muscle architecture in N-terminal mutants (Figure 4E).

claim: The strongest form of evidence supporting causality of a mutation is whether it results in a truncation of the protein for genes where loss-of-function mutations are known to cause disease.
source: Recent guidance issued by the American College of Medical Genetics emphasizes that the strongest form of evidence supporting causality of a mutation is whether it results in a truncation of the protein (nonsense, frameshift or canonical splice-site mutations), specifically for genes where loss-of-function mutations are known to cause disease (Richards et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from Richards et al., 2015.

claim: Truncating mutations within alternatively spliced exons and at the extreme C-terminus of the protein must be interpreted with caution, as they may have little to no impact on protein function.
source: Truncating mutations within alternatively spliced exons and at the extreme C-terminus of the protein must be interpreted with caution, as they may have little to no impact on protein function.
evidence: This is stated as part of the ACMG guidelines discussion.

claim: TTN lies along the length of the sarcomere and is thought to mediate passive tension of the muscle fiber.
source: TTN lies along the length of the sarcomere and is thought to mediate passive tension of the muscle fiber, while also serving as a binding scaffold for a large number of proteins, including actin and myosin (Lewinter and Granzier, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Lewinter and Granzier, 2013.

claim: TTN serves as a binding scaffold for a large number of proteins, including actin and myosin.
source: TTN lies along the length of the sarcomere and is thought to mediate passive tension of the muscle fiber, while also serving as a binding scaffold for a large number of proteins, including actin and myosin (Lewinter and Granzier, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from Lewinter and Granzier, 2013.

claim: Individual regions of TTN are annotated according to their localization to the Z-disc, I-band, A-band, and M-line regions of the sarcomere visualized on immuno-electron micrographs.
source: Individual regions of TTN are annotated according to their localization to the Z-disc, I-band, A-band, and M-line regions of the sarcomere visualized on immuno-electron micrographs Fürst et al., 1988.
evidence: This is cited from Fürst et al., 1988.

claim: Truncating and/or missense mutations in TTN result in cardiac (dilated cardiomyopathy [DCM]) and skeletal muscle (myofibrillar myopathy) disease.
source: Truncating and/or missense mutations in TTN result in cardiac (dilated cardiomyopathy [DCM]) and skeletal muscle (myofibrillar myopathy) disease (Chauveau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Chauveau et al., 2014.

claim: Truncation mutations in TTN may explain as much as 25% of DCM.
source: Recent estimates suggest that truncation mutations in TTN may explain as much as 25% of DCM (Herman et al., 2012), a disease which affects upwards of 1 in 2500 individuals (Codd et al., 1989).
evidence: This is cited from Herman et al., 2012.

claim: DCM affects upwards of 1 in 2500 individuals.
source: Recent estimates suggest that truncation mutations in TTN may explain as much as 25% of DCM (Herman et al., 2012), a disease which affects upwards of 1 in 2500 individuals (Codd et al., 1989).
evidence: This is cited from Codd et al., 1989.

claim: In patients with the most severe forms of DCM, truncations reside within the C-terminal two-thirds of the protein (from amino acid 14,760 onwards), specifically in the distal I-band and A-band.
source: Although truncations are found along the length of TTN in DCM patients, in patients with the most severe forms of DCM, truncations reside within the C-terminal two-thirds of the protein (from amino acid 14,760 onwards, Figure 1A), specifically in the distal I-band and A-band (we will refer to these as C-terminal truncations) (Herman et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Herman et al., 2012 and Roberts et al., 2015, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Multiple TTN exons are alternatively spliced.
source: Multiple TTN exons are alternatively spliced (Bang et al., 2001), with many having little to no inclusion within cardiac isoforms, and splicing has been proposed to at least partially explain the exclusion of N-terminal mutations in patients with end-stage DCM (Herman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Bang et al., 2001.

claim: Over 5500 amino acids in the N-terminal region of the protein are constitutive (PSI >0.9).
source: Nonetheless, over 5500 amino acids in the N-terminal region of the protein are constitutive (percent spliced in or PSI >0.9, Figure 1B), implying the importance of other mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Zebrafish has high sequence conservation of sarcomeric proteins with mammals and recapitulate disease phenotypes with loss-of-function of multiple established Mendelian cardiomyopathy genes.
source: Firstly, zebrafish has high sequence conservation of sarcomeric proteins with mammals and recapitulate disease phenotypes with loss-of-function of multiple established Mendelian cardiomyopathy genes (Dahme et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from Dahme et al., 2009.

claim: Forward genetic screens have generated zebrafish Titin mutants, although in only one case is the position of the mutation known.
source: In fact, forward genetic screens have generated zebrafish Titin mutants, although in only one case is the position of the mutation known (Xu et al., 2002; Steffen et al., 2007; Myhre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Xu et al., 2002; Steffen et al., 2007; Myhre et al., 2014.

claim: Zebrafish can live for up to two weeks with a non-contractile heart.
source: Secondly, zebrafish can live for up to two weeks with a non-contractile heart, thus allowing mechanistic studies of homozygote mutants.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of zebrafish.

claim: Zebrafish include two titin genes: ttna and ttnb as a result of an ancestral genome duplication event.
source: As a result of an ancestral genome duplication event, zebrafish include two titin genes: ttna and ttnb (Xu et al., 2002; Steffen et al., 2007; Seeley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Xu et al., 2002; Steffen et al., 2007; Seeley et al., 2007.

claim: Zebrafish ttna shares 56% identity and 82% homology with human TTN.
source: Ttna shares considerable similarity with the human TTN gene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, showing 'meta-transcripts' with all possible exons included). The zebrafish and human proteins are similar in length (∼32,000–35,000 amino acids depending on the splice isoform) and share 56% identity and 82% homology.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Zebrafish and human TTN proteins are similar in length (∼32,000–35,000 amino acids depending on the splice isoform).
source: The zebrafish and human proteins are similar in length (∼32,000–35,000 amino acids depending on the splice isoform) and share 56% identity and 82% homology.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Zebrafish and human TTN have a nearly identical domain organization, with three immunoglobulin-like domains, an elastic PEVK region, N2A and N2B domains, a fibronectin-immunoglobulin repeat region, and a C-terminal kinase domain.
source: They have a nearly identical domain organization, with three immunoglobulin-like of domains (proximal, mid, and distal), an elastic PEVK region, N2A and N2B domains which distinguish cardiac and skeletal isoforms, a fibronectin-immunoglobulin repeat region that mediates binding to myosin, and a C-terminal kinase domain.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison.

claim: Alternative splicing targets the middle Ig-like and PEVK domains in both zebrafish and human TTN, which modulate passive tensile properties of the sarcomere.
source: In both species, alternative splicing targets the middle Ig-like and PEVK domains, which modulate passive tensile properties of the sarcomere (Granzier and Labeit, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Granzier and Labeit, 2004.

claim: Cardiac isoforms typically include much of the elastic region as well as the N2B ± N2A domains.
source: Cardiac isoforms typically include much of this elastic region as well as the N2B ± N2A domains, while skeletal isoforms include the N2A domain but exclude N2B as well as much of the elastic region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TTN isoforms.

claim: Skeletal isoforms include the N2A domain but exclude N2B as well as much of the elastic region.
source: Cardiac isoforms typically include much of this elastic region as well as the N2B ± N2A domains, while skeletal isoforms include the N2A domain but exclude N2B as well as much of the elastic region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TTN isoforms.

claim: ttna is essential for cardiac sarcomere formation in zebrafish.
source: Multiple mutants isolated from forward genetic screens coupled with morpholino knockdown analysis have demonstrated that ttna is essential for cardiac sarcomere formation in zebrafish (Xu et al., 2002; Myhre et al., 2014; Seeley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Xu et al., 2002; Myhre et al., 2014; Seeley et al., 2007.

claim: The zebrafish ttnb gene is dispensable for cardiac sarcomere development.
source: Although the paralagous zebrafish ttnb gene is dispensable for cardiac sarcomere development (Steffen et al., 2007; Seeley et al., 2007), it plays an essential role in skeletal muscle sarcomerogenesis.
evidence: This is cited from Steffen et al., 2007; Seeley et al., 2007.

claim: ttnb plays an essential role in skeletal muscle sarcomerogenesis.
source: Although the paralagous zebrafish ttnb gene is dispensable for cardiac sarcomere development (Steffen et al., 2007; Seeley et al., 2007), it plays an essential role in skeletal muscle sarcomerogenesis.
evidence: This is cited from Steffen et al., 2007; Seeley et al., 2007.

claim: ttnb is expressed at comparable levels to ttna in skeletal muscle.
source: It is expressed at comparable levels to ttna in skeletal muscle (as opposed to ∼2/3 of ttna abundance in heart).
evidence: This is based on expression analysis.

claim: The ttnb protein has abbreviated versions of the middle Ig-like and PEVK elastic domains compared to human TTN or zebrafish ttna.
source: In contrast to human TTN or zebrafish ttna, the ttnb protein has abbreviated versions of the middle Ig-like and PEVK elastic domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and thus more closely resembles skeletal rather than cardiac muscle isoforms of ttna.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Morpholino-based skipping of the N2A exon of either ttna or ttnb results in severe disruption of skeletal muscle sarcomeric architecture.
source: Morpholino-based skipping of the N2A exon of either ttna or ttnb results in severe disruption of skeletal muscle sarcomeric architecture, highlighting the mutual contribution of the two genes (Seeley et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Seeley et al., 2007.

claim: Six truncating mutations were engineered within ttna at the Z-disk (n1), proximal or mid I-band (n2 and n3) or proximal, mid, or distal A-band (c1, c2, and c3).
source: Using CRISPR/Cas9 technology (Jinek et al., 2012), we engineered six truncating mutations within the major cardiac TTN orthologue, ttna, (Figure 1A, Table 1), so that the resulting protein product would be truncated at either the Z-disk (n1), proximal or mid I-band (n2 and n3) or proximal, mid, or distal A-band (c1, c2, and c3).
evidence: This is described in the Results section and detailed in Table 1.

claim: All targeted exons were anticipated to be constitutive in both cardiac and skeletal muscle (PSI >0.99) based on wild-type zebrafish embryo transcriptome data.
source: From wild-type (WT) zebrafish embryo transcriptome data, we anticipated that all exons would be constitutive in both cardiac and skeletal muscle (PSI >0.99, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: ttna truncations showed no gross phenotype in heterozygotes, with all heterozygotes attaining sexual maturity.
source: As expected (Xu et al., 2002; Gramlich et al., 2015), ttna truncations showed no gross phenotype in heterozygotes, with all heterozygotes attaining sexual maturity.
evidence: This is based on observation of the mutant lines and cited from Xu et al., 2002; Gramlich et al., 2015.

claim: N-terminal and C-terminal truncations all showed severe deficits in cardiac contractility.
source: N-terminal (ttnan1/n1, ttnan2/n2, ttnan3/n3, collectively referred to as ttnan/n) and C-terminal (ttnac/c) truncations all showed severe deficits in cardiac contractility (Video 1) and typically died within two weeks of birth.
evidence: This is shown in Video 1 and described in the Results.

claim: ttna homozygote mutants typically died within two weeks of birth.
source: N-terminal (ttnan1/n1, ttnan2/n2, ttnan3/n3, collectively referred to as ttnan/n) and C-terminal (ttnac/c) truncations all showed severe deficits in cardiac contractility (Video 1) and typically died within two weeks of birth.
evidence: This is based on observation of the mutant lines.

claim: Immunostaining revealed severe cardiac sarcomeric disarray in all ttna mutants.
source: Immunostaining revealed severe cardiac sarcomeric disarray (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All three ttnan/n mutants were capable of grossly normal motion.
source: In contrast to their cardiac phenotypes, ttna mutants demonstrated a sharp division in development of skeletal muscle disease. All three ttnan/n mutants were capable of grossly normal motion while the ttnac/c truncations were entirely unable to move (Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Video 2.

claim: ttnac/c truncations were entirely unable to move.
source: In contrast to their cardiac phenotypes, ttna mutants demonstrated a sharp division in development of skeletal muscle disease. All three ttnan/n mutants were capable of grossly normal motion while the ttnac/c truncations were entirely unable to move (Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Video 2.

claim: ttnac/c mutants had highly distorted sarcomeric architecture while ttnan/n architecture closely resembled wild-type.
source: Immunostaining supported the distinction, with ttnac/c mutants having highly distorted sarcomeric architecture while ttnan/n architecture closely resembled wild-type (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B through immunostaining for α-actinin.

claim: All mutated exons appeared constitutive in both heart and skeletal muscle, across all genotypes.
source: To confirm transcription of all mutant isoforms, assess nonsense-mediated decay, and rule out selective alternative splicing of ttnan/n mutant exons, we performed RNA-Seq of heart (cardiac muscle) and trunk (skeletal muscle) of 3 day old embryos, as well as adult fish. All mutated exons appeared constitutive in both heart and skeletal muscle, across all genotypes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C through RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Approximately 75–80% of mutant transcript was degraded by nonsense-mediated decay.
source: We next examined the extent of nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) for each mutant allele by performing targeted RNA sequencing of heterozygote embryos and comparing the number of reads for wild-type and mutant exons. In keeping with typical estimates for NMD efficiency (Zetoune et al., 2008), we saw ∼75–80% of mutant transcript being degraded (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and cited from Zetoune et al., 2008.

claim: No substantial variation in nonsense-mediated decay efficiency was seen across the mutants.
source: In keeping with typical estimates for NMD efficiency (Zetoune et al., 2008), we saw ∼75–80% of mutant transcript being degraded (Figure 2D). However, no substantial variation was seen across the mutants.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Knockdown of ttnb by morpholino disrupted ttnan/n skeletal muscle morphology.
source: Knockdown of ttnb by morpholino disrupted ttnan/n skeletal muscle morphology indicating that the intact skeletal muscle sarcomeric architecture in ttnan/n mutants arose at least in part from rescue by ttnb protein (Figure 3A), although the phenotype was not nearly as severe as that of ttnac/c mutants.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A through immunostaining.

claim: The intact skeletal muscle sarcomeric architecture in ttnan/n mutants arose at least in part from rescue by ttnb protein.
source: Knockdown of ttnb by morpholino disrupted ttnan/n skeletal muscle morphology indicating that the intact skeletal muscle sarcomeric architecture in ttnan/n mutants arose at least in part from rescue by ttnb protein (Figure 3A), although the phenotype was not nearly as severe as that of ttnac/c mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the morpholino knockdown experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Morpholino knockdown of ttna was unable to rescue skeletal muscle architecture in ttnac/c mutants.
source: Knockdown by morpholino was effective (∼78% knockdown efficiency, data not shown) and the combined action of NMD and morpholino knockdown would be expected to reduce mutant ttna protein to only ∼5% of the level of ttnb protein. Nonetheless we were unable to rescue skeletal muscle architecture in ttnac/c mutants (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through immunostaining.

claim: ttnac/c mutants do not act as dominant negatives.
source: We thus concluded that ttnac/c mutants do not act as dominant negatives and that an alternative explanation was needed.
evidence: This is inferred from the failure to rescue skeletal muscle architecture by introducing an upstream frameshift (Figure 3B).

claim: An accumulation of reads 5' to exon 116 was observed in zebrafish skeletal muscle RNA-Seq data.
source: Using the exon boundaries defined by ttnan3/n3 and ttnac1/c1, we examined zebrafish and mouse cardiac and skeletal muscle transcriptomic data for patterns of reads indicating a promoter upstream of one of the ttna exons. We noticed an accumulation of reads 5' to exon 116 (e116, ENSDART00000109099) in zebrafish skeletal muscle (Figure 4A) and in the corresponding exon of mouse heart (e223, ENSMUST00000099981, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: An accumulation of reads was observed in the corresponding exon of mouse heart (e223).
source: We noticed an accumulation of reads 5' to exon 116 (e116, ENSDART00000109099) in zebrafish skeletal muscle (Figure 4A) and in the corresponding exon of mouse heart (e223, ENSMUST00000099981, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A through RNA-Seq data analysis.

claim: 5'-RACE confirmed an alternative transcription start site 110 bp upstream of e116 (within the e115-e116 intron) in zebrafish skeletal muscle.
source: 5'-RACE confirmed an alternative transcription start site (TSS), 110 bp upstream of e116 (within the e115-e116 intron) in zebrafish skeletal muscle, with an in-frame initiator methionine located 7 amino acids upstream of e116.
evidence: This is based on 5'-RACE experiments described in the Methods.

claim: An in-frame initiator methionine is located 7 amino acids upstream of e116 in zebrafish.
source: 5'-RACE confirmed an alternative transcription start site (TSS), 110 bp upstream of e116 (within the e115-e116 intron) in zebrafish skeletal muscle, with an in-frame initiator methionine located 7 amino acids upstream of e116.
evidence: This is based on 5'-RACE experiments and sequence analysis.

claim: A TSS was found 257bp upstream of e223 in mouse cardiac tissue.
source: To establish conservation in mammals, we repeated 5'-RACE on adult mouse and fetal human cardiac tissue and found a TSS in the upstream intron (257bp upstream of e223 in mouse; 256bp upstream of the orthologous exon, e240, in humans), with a putative initiator methionine 12 amino acids upstream of the relevant exon.
evidence: This is based on 5'-RACE experiments on mouse tissue.

claim: A TSS was found 256bp upstream of e240 in human cardiac tissue.
source: To establish conservation in mammals, we repeated 5'-RACE on adult mouse and fetal human cardiac tissue and found a TSS in the upstream intron (257bp upstream of e223 in mouse; 256bp upstream of the orthologous exon, e240, in humans), with a putative initiator methionine 12 amino acids upstream of the relevant exon.
evidence: This is based on 5'-RACE experiments on human tissue.

claim: A putative initiator methionine is located 12 amino acids upstream of the relevant exon in mammals.
source: To establish conservation in mammals, we repeated 5'-RACE on adult mouse and fetal human cardiac tissue and found a TSS in the upstream intron (257bp upstream of e223 in mouse; 256bp upstream of the orthologous exon, e240, in humans), with a putative initiator methionine 12 amino acids upstream of the relevant exon.
evidence: This is based on 5'-RACE experiments and sequence analysis.

claim: PCR confirmed the presence of a multi-exonic transcript that includes the alternative promoter site in zebrafish, mouse, and human cardiac tissue.
source: Using PCR, we confirmed the presence of a multi-exonic transcript that includes this alternative promoter site in zebrafish, mouse, and human cardiac tissue (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B through PCR amplification.

claim: DNAse-Seq data revealed a prominent peak overlying e240 in multiple fetal human cardiac and skeletal muscle datasets.
source: Examination of multiple fetal human cardiac and skeletal muscle DNA-Seq datasets revealed a prominent peak overlying e240, the orthologous exon to e116 in humans (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 through analysis of publicly available DNAse-Seq data.

claim: A similar peak was found in H3K4me3 Chip-Seq data from skeletal muscle and cardiac tissue.
source: A similar peak was found in H3K4me3 Chip-Seq data, a mark for active promoters (Zhou et al., 2010), from skeletal muscle and cardiac tissue (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 through analysis of publicly available ChIP-Seq data, and cited from Zhou et al., 2010.

claim: The corresponding human genomic position (the e239-e240 intron) represents the exact transition point for where disease severity markedly increases in DCM TTN truncation patients.
source: Interestingly, the corresponding human genomic position (the e239-e240 intron in ENST00000589042) represents the exact transition point for where disease severity markedly increases in DCM TTN truncation patients (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A comparing the internal promoter position with patient mutation data.

claim: e113, e114 and e115 F0 mutants showed intact skeletal muscle architecture.
source: As expected, e113, e114 and e115 F0 mutants showed intact skeletal muscle architecture while e116 and e122 mutants had severe skeletal muscle disruption (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 through immunostaining.

claim: e116 and e122 mutants had severe skeletal muscle disruption.
source: As expected, e113, e114 and e115 F0 mutants showed intact skeletal muscle architecture while e116 and e122 mutants had severe skeletal muscle disruption (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 through immunostaining.

claim: A higher mobility (smaller size) protein product was found in wild-type and ttnan/n mutants but not in ttnac/c mutants.
source: To confirm that the Cronos isoform protein product was actually translated, we used agarose protein electrophoresis and found that a higher mobility (smaller size) protein product was indeed found in wild-type and ttnan/n mutants but not in ttnac/c mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A through protein gel electrophoresis.

claim: A translation start site morpholino targeted upstream of the alternative initiator methionine was sufficient to completely impair motility and disrupt skeletal muscle architecture in the ttnan3/n3 mutant.
source: Finally, a translation start site morpholino targeted upstream of the actual alternative initiator methionine (and 38 nucleotides upstream of the intron-exon junction) was sufficient to completely impair motility and disrupt skeletal muscle architecture in the ttnan3/n3 mutant (Figure 4E, Video 3), further supporting the hypothesis that the Cronos product can rescue skeletal muscle architecture in ttnan/n mutants.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and Video 3 through morpholino knockdown experiments.

claim: A much higher ratio of Cronos:full-length transcript levels was observed in ttnan/n mutants than in ttnac/c mutants.
source: In ttnan/n mutants, which would degrade full-length ttna but not Cronos, we would anticipate a higher Cronos:full-length ratio than in ttnac/c mutants mutants, which should degrade both transcripts approximately equally. As expected, we see a much higher ratio of Cronos:full-length transcript levels in ttnan/n mutants than in ttnac/c mutants (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B through quantitative real-time PCR.

claim: Cronos is expressed at high levels in zebrafish skeletal muscle during development (∼2:1 ratio of Cronos to full-length ttna).
source: Cronos is expressed at high levels in zebrafish skeletal muscle during development (∼2:1 ratio of Cronos to full-length ttna), but drops off sharply during adulthood (∼1:70 ratio).
evidence: This is shown through in situ hybridization (Figure 6A) and real-time PCR (Figure 6B).

claim: Cronos expression drops off sharply during adulthood in zebrafish skeletal muscle (∼1:70 ratio).
source: Cronos is expressed at high levels in zebrafish skeletal muscle during development (∼2:1 ratio of Cronos to full-length ttna), but drops off sharply during adulthood (∼1:70 ratio).
evidence: This is shown through real-time PCR (Figure 6B).

claim: Cronos expression in zebrafish heart is much lower than in skeletal muscle, with a ∼1:5 ratio at 72 hpf and 1:30 ratio in adulthood.
source: Although the Cronos expression in zebrafish heart also appears to be developmentally regulated, it is much lower than in skeletal muscle, with a ∼1:5 ratio at 72 hpf and 1:30 ratio in adulthood.
evidence: This is shown through in situ hybridization (Figure 6A) and real-time PCR (Figure 6B).

claim: Low cardiac Cronos expression (coupled with a minor role of ttnb in zebrafish hearts) is a likely reason for the severe and indistinguishable cardiac sarcomere disruption in ttnan/n and ttnac/c mutants.
source: This low cardiac Cronos expression (coupled with a minor role of ttnb in zebrafish hearts) is a likely reason for the severe and indistinguishable cardiac sarcomere disruption in ttnan/n and ttnac/c mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data and phenotypic observations.

claim: Cronos levels were much higher in developing mouse hearts than in zebrafish, with nearly equal transcript levels of Cronos and full-length Ttn at embryonic day 12.5.
source: We found that Cronos levels were much higher in developing mouse hearts than in zebrafish, with nearly equal transcript levels of Cronos and full-length Ttn (Figure 6C) at embryonic day 12.5.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C through quantitative PCR.

claim: Mouse cardiac expression of Cronos decreases to ∼20–30% of full-length Titin after embryonic day 12.5.
source: Thereafter mouse cardiac expression of Cronos decreases to ∼20–30% of full-length Titin.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C through quantitative PCR.

claim: Skeletal muscle Cronos expression varies across development and in different muscle beds with a 1:5 ratio in mouse hindlimb at P2.
source: Skeletal muscle expression varies across development and in different muscle beds with a 1:5 ratio in mouse hindlimb at P2, and between 1:16 and ∼1:1000 ratios in adult extensor digitorum longus (fast-twitch) and soleus (slow-twitch) muscle, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C through quantitative PCR.

claim: Adult extensor digitorum longus (fast-twitch) muscle has a Cronos to full-length Ttn ratio between 1:16.
source: Skeletal muscle expression varies across development and in different muscle beds with a 1:5 ratio in mouse hindlimb at P2, and between 1:16 and ∼1:1000 ratios in adult extensor digitorum longus (fast-twitch) and soleus (slow-twitch) muscle, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C through quantitative PCR.

claim: Adult soleus (slow-twitch) muscle has a Cronos to full-length Ttn ratio of approximately 1:1000.
source: Skeletal muscle expression varies across development and in different muscle beds with a 1:5 ratio in mouse hindlimb at P2, and between 1:16 and ∼1:1000 ratios in adult extensor digitorum longus (fast-twitch) and soleus (slow-twitch) muscle, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C through quantitative PCR.

claim: The complete TTN exome of 199 competitive senior athletes was sequenced along with 104 other Mendelian cardiac disease genes.
source: To assess whether any TTN truncations are compatible with a high degree of cardiovascular fitness throughout life, we turned to a population genetics approach, and sequenced the complete TTN exome (as well as that of 104 other Mendelian cardiac disease genes, Supplementary file 1A) in 199 competitive senior athletes who entered as contestants in the Huntsman World Senior Games (median age 73, Table 2).
evidence: This is described in the Results section.

claim: The overall rate of TTN truncations did not differ between senior athletes and CTLlit (1.5 vs 1.2%, p = 0.91).
source: The overall rate of TTN truncations did not differ between senior athletes and CTLlit (1.5 vs 1.2%, p = 0.91).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of sequencing data.

claim: The distribution of TTN truncations differed significantly between senior athletes and CTLlit.
source: However, the distribution of TTN truncations differed significantly between groups (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1): TTN truncations in senior athletes mapped exclusively to the extreme C-terminal exon of the rare Novex-3 isoform (Bang et al., 2001), at a nearly 8-fold higher rate than CTLlit (p = 0.003).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 through statistical analysis.

claim: TTN truncations in senior athletes mapped exclusively to the extreme C-terminal exon of the rare Novex-3 isoform at a nearly 8-fold higher rate than CTLlit (p = 0.003).

evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 through statistical analysis and cited from Bang et al., 2001.

claim: The Novex-3 exon is found only in the Novex-3 isoform, which is expressed at low levels in the human heart (<10% of the levels of major TTN isoforms).
source: This exon is found only in the Novex-3 isoform, which is expressed at low levels in the human heart (<10% of the levels of major TTN isoforms [Roberts et al., 2015]), and we would thus expect truncations in this exon would have little effect on TTN function.
evidence: This is cited from Roberts et al., 2015.

claim: In end-stage DCM, a much higher rate of mutants C-terminal to Cronos than N-terminal was observed (30:1).
source: As expected, in end-stage DCM we observed a much higher rate of mutants C-terminal to Cronos than N-terminal (30:1), followed by unselected DCM (37:11), literature controls (6:11, 2:2, 10:7 for FHS, healthy volunteers and JHS) and senior athletes (0:3).

claim: In unselected DCM, the ratio of C-terminal to N-terminal mutants was 37:11.
source: As expected, in end-stage DCM we observed a much higher rate of mutants C-terminal to Cronos than N-terminal (30:1), followed by unselected DCM (37:11), literature controls (6:11, 2:2, 10:7 for FHS, healthy volunteers and JHS) and senior athletes (0:3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 through analysis of mutation distribution.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 through analysis of mutation distribution.

claim: Loss of function experiments across a number of systems have demonstrated Titin's importance in diverse aspects of sarcomere development and function.
source: Loss of function experiments across a number of systems have demonstrated Titin's importance in diverse aspects of sarcomere development and function, including the ordered assembly of sarcomeric constituents (Xu et al., 2002; van der Ven et al., 2000), cardiomyocyte systolic (Hinson et al., 2015) and diastolic function (Radke et al., 2007), and resistance to neurohormonal and vasoconstrictor stresses (Gramlich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Xu et al., 2002; van der Ven et al., 2000; Hinson et al., 2015; Radke et al., 2007; Gramlich et al., 2009.

claim: The Cronos protein product is essential for skeletal muscle sarcomere development in zebrafish.
source: Our work further contributes the discovery of a conserved internal promoter in TTN, whose protein product is essential for skeletal muscle sarcomere development in zebrafish.
evidence: This is demonstrated through morpholino knockdown experiments (Figure 4E) and phenotypic analysis.

claim: The Cronos promoter is prominently expressed in developing mouse heart.
source: The Cronos promoter is prominently expressed in developing mouse heart, and its location coincides strikingly with the position of TTN truncations in patients with the most severe forms of dilated cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This is shown through quantitative PCR (Figure 6C).

claim: The location of the Cronos promoter coincides strikingly with the position of TTN truncations in patients with the most severe forms of dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: The Cronos promoter is prominently expressed in developing mouse heart, and its location coincides strikingly with the position of TTN truncations in patients with the most severe forms of dilated cardiomyopathy.
evidence: This is shown by comparing the internal promoter position with patient mutation data (Figure 1A).

claim: Disruption of both the full-length TTN and Cronos protein products results in more severe disease than disruption of the full-length product alone.
source: Our working model is that disruption of both the full-length TTN and Cronos protein products results in more severe disease than disruption of the full-length product alone.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The mode of inheritance in TTN truncation mutation patients is heterozygous with marked variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
source: With the exception of certain childhood-onset forms of skeletal and cardiac myopathy arising from homozygous TTN truncations (Carmignac et al., 2007; Ceyhan-Birsoy et al., 2013), the mode of inheritance in TTN truncation mutation patients is heterozygous with marked variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance (Herman et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2015; Itoh-Satoh et al., 2002; Norton et al., 2013; van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from multiple sources: Carmignac et al., 2007; Ceyhan-Birsoy et al., 2013; Herman et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2015; Itoh-Satoh et al., 2002; Norton et al., 2013; van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al., 2014.

claim: Disease onset in TTN truncation patients usually occurs in adulthood.
source: Moreover, disease onset usually occurs in adulthood.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of TTN truncation mutations.

claim: Strategies that augment activity of the internal TTN promoter and levels of the Cronos isoform might provide therapeutic benefit in TTN truncation patients.
source: Secondly, our work implies that strategies that augment activity of the internal TTN promoter and levels of the Cronos isoform might provide therapeutic benefit in TTN truncation patients, although it is unclear whether there is a restricted developmental window where this might be possible.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic implication based on the findings.

claim: The thin/thick filament arrangement in the sarcomere alters its geometry, progressing from a tetragonal lattice arrangement at the Z-band to a trigonal arrangement in the A-band.
source: Electron microscopy reconstructions of serial sections of skeletal muscle dating back over 50 years presented a puzzle: the thin/thick filament arrangement in the sarcomere alters its geometry, progressing from a tetragonal lattice arrangement at the Z-band to a trigonal arrangement in the A-band (Pringle, 1968), with the transition taking place near the I-A junction (Traeger et al., 1983).
evidence: This is cited from Pringle, 1968 and Traeger et al., 1983.

claim: The transition from tetragonal to trigonal lattice arrangement takes place near the I-A junction.
source: Electron microscopy reconstructions of serial sections of skeletal muscle dating back over 50 years presented a puzzle: the thin/thick filament arrangement in the sarcomere alters its geometry, progressing from a tetragonal lattice arrangement at the Z-band to a trigonal arrangement in the A-band (Pringle, 1968), with the transition taking place near the I-A junction (Traeger et al., 1983).
evidence: This is cited from Traeger et al., 1983.

claim: The implication for TTN would be that there would be a resulting increase in the copies of TTN protein, with four at the Z-band and six at the A-band and M-line.
source: The implication for TTN would be that there would be a resulting increase in the copies of TTN protein, with four at the Z-band and six at the A-band and M-line (Liversage et al., 2001), which is difficult to reconcile with the fact that a single TTN molecule spans the entire length, from Z-band to M-line.
evidence: This is cited from Liversage et al., 2001.

claim: The Cronos protein product selectively increases copies of TTN at the distal I-band, A-band and M-line.
source: Our data provides a simple explanation for this observation, with the Cronos protein product selectively increasing copies of TTN at the distal I-band, A-band and M-line.
evidence: This is inferred from the discovery of the Cronos isoform and its expression pattern.

claim: The T2 band on protein gels migrates at the expected molecular weight of Cronos.
source: Our work also proposes an alternative explanation for the consistently observed 'T2' band on protein gels, which migrates at the expected molecular weight of Cronos.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the observed T2 band with the Cronos isoform.

claim: The T2 band has invariably been labeled a C-terminal degradation product, as it reacts with A-band antibodies.
source: This has invariably been labeled a C-terminal degradation product, as it reacts with A-band antibodies (Opitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Opitz et al., 2004.

claim: The T2 band was prominently seen in developing mouse and rat hearts, but was markedly reduced in adulthood.
source: However, in keeping with Cronos expression patterns in development, the T2 band was prominently seen in developing mouse (Lahmers et al., 2004) and rat hearts (Opitz et al., 2004), but was markedly reduced in adulthood.
